scenario.title: SVC system call path - privilege round trip, an ignored cpsid and a forbidden SysTick write
scenario.description: Tasks run unprivileged on the PSP. Task C prints "C" through "svc #3" (write): the core enters handler mode (privileged, MSP), the SVC handler reads the SVC number from the svc instruction just before the stacked PC, takes the argument from the stacked r0, writes the UART, puts the return value into the stacked r0 and returns to unprivileged thread mode. On its third iteration C tries two privileged things directly. "cpsid i" is silently ignored, exactly as on the real core (PRIMASK stays 0, no fault). The write to SYST_CSR is an unprivileged access to the System Control Space: a precise BusFault with BFAR = 0xE000E010. The kernel kills C; A and B continue.

expected.summary: Several svc write calls succeed with a privilege round trip each; cpsid in task C is ignored; the SysTick write is a precise BusFault (BFAR=0xE000E010); C is DEAD, A and B keep running, no lockup.

scenario.what_to_look_for: For each system call: a cpu syscall event "svc #3 from unprivileged thread (r0=0x00000043)", an exception_entry SVCall whose stacked frame holds the argument in r0 and the return address in pc, a kernel syscall event that says where the SVC number came from (stacked PC - 4) and that the return value 1 was written to the stacked r0, and an exception_return "back to thread mode (unprivileged)". Then a marker "taskC: trying a privileged operation directly", a privilege event "'cpsid' ignored" (no fault, PRIMASK unchanged), and a fault event: BusFault PRECISERR at the "str r1, [r0]" instruction, privileged=false, context C, BFAR=0xE000E010 (SYST_CSR). The task_state event says C is DEAD and a context_switch moves on. The kernel event at scheduler start (CONTROL=3) is where the privilege drop happened.
likely_root_causes: A task calls a kernel function directly instead of through SVC: with CONTROL.nPRIV set, NVIC/SysTick/SCB/MPU registers give a BusFault and cpsid/cpsie/msr are ignored.
The SVC handler reads arguments from the live r0-r3 instead of the stacked frame; and the return value must be written to the stacked r0 (see P17).
The handler picks the wrong stack (MSP vs PSP) when locating the frame; test EXC_RETURN bit 2 (tst lr, #4).
The SVC number is read from the wrong place: it is the immediate of the svc instruction at (stacked PC - 2) for the 16-bit Thumb encoding, not a register.
how_to_debug: Break in the SVC handler: 'p/x $lr' (EXC_RETURN), then 'x/8xw $psp'. r0 must be the argument and the stacked PC must point just after the svc instruction ('x/i <stacked pc> - 2').
Read CONTROL from the task ('mrs r0, control' or 'p $control' in GDB): bit 0 = 1 means unprivileged, bit 1 = 1 means PSP.
Put cpsid i in a task on real hardware and read PRIMASK afterwards ('p $primask'): it stays 0, proving the instruction was ignored.
Decode the BusFault: CFSR (0xE000ED28) shows PRECISERR+BFARVALID, BFAR (0xE000ED38) = 0xE000E010, and the stacked PC is the store that tried to write SysTick.
scenario.what_this_means: SVC is the only door from an unprivileged task into the kernel: the hardware raises the privilege on entry and drops it again on return, and arguments and results travel through the stacked frame. Anything a task tries to do directly that needs privilege either fails loudly (BusFault on the System Control Space) or silently (cpsid ignored). Either way the kernel's state is protected, which is the reason tasks run unprivileged.
scenario.hidden_symptom: A task that tries to disable interrupts has no effect at all; the same task dies with a BusFault when it touches SysTick.
